title: The Growing Heap
subtitle: Memory rises after every request and never returns

brief.narrative: A global dictionary stores request objects by trace ID with no eviction. Garbage collection cannot reclaim objects that remain reachable.
symptoms: Application Heap metrics diverge from the service-level symptom
The problem reproduces only under the triggering workload
Logs contain enough evidence to distinguish cause from consequence
brief.objective: Identify the root cause, select a production-safe fix, and explain the trade-off.

rootCause.question: Which root cause explains all of the evidence?

options.text: Opposite lock ordering created a circular wait.
options.feedback: This choice does not explain the complete evidence or leaves the underlying correctness/reliability problem intact.

options.text: CPython’s GIL serializes execution of Python bytecode for CPU-bound threads.
options.feedback: This choice does not explain the complete evidence or leaves the underlying correctness/reliability problem intact.

options.text: An unbounded retained-reference cache caused a memory leak.
options.feedback: Correct. A leak is about unintended reachability, not merely high allocation. RSS may also stay high because allocators retain arenas.

options.text: A data race on a non-atomic shared counter caused lost increments.
options.feedback: This choice does not explain the complete evidence or leaves the underlying correctness/reliability problem intact.

fix.question: Which fix is safest for production?

options.text: Use multiprocessing, a native library that releases the GIL, or a separate compute service; benchmark serialization and memory costs.
options.feedback: This choice does not explain the complete evidence or leaves the underlying correctness/reliability problem intact.

options.text: Bound the cache with size/TTL, remove entries at lifecycle completion, and compare heap profiles by retained path.
